We never reached the far wall that summer, though Dario spoke of it each morning as if distance were only another word to learn. He sat on the rim of the salt pool in Havana, trousers rolled, and named things in the language of his village: tile, gull, the green rust on the ladder. Bartolo repeated each word and swam a length before the next. On Thursday she stopped short of the far wall, held the rope, and came back saying she had only wanted to rest. Dario nodded and gave her the word for rest, then a second, older word that he said meant resting before one has finished. She practiced it without asking why. Later, reciting the colors, he paused at the word for the rust, and let her supply it, which she did loudly, as though he had been testing her. On the walk home she carried his towel over her shoulder, still damp at one corner where the rope had dripped on it.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the passage?

Once, near the end of my nights at the pharmacy in Lima, Valentina came in at two in the morning and did not ask for anything on the shelves. For six years she had sent me her chapters typed, never handwritten; the notebooks she kept locked in a drawer her own sister had never seen. That week a colleague had told me, kindly and wrongly, that Valentina was talking to a translator in Madrid. I said as much while I rang up the mints she finally chose. She looked at the fluorescent tubes and remarked that they made everyone look like a ghost of themselves. Then she set a green notebook on the counter, its pages crowded with her slanted ink and crossed-out lines, and said she would collect it Thursday. I put it under the register, beside the night ledger, and kept my hand on its cover until the bell over the door stopped swinging.

Flour dusted my stepmother's wrists before the sun was up, and by five she had already shaped forty loaves for an oven she could no longer afford to repair. I was sixteen and had told her, more than once, that the bakery in our Tbilisi lane was finished: the new supermarket sold bread cheaper, and Stanislav, who had fired the oven for my father, was nearly eighty. She never argued. She only set out cups of tea each morning, one for herself and one for Stanislav, and a third, untouched, at my place on the bench. __One morning I sat down and drank it, and she slid the scoring blade across the table toward me without a word.__ I cut the loaves badly. Stanislav laughed until he coughed. Dmitri, my friend from school, asked that afternoon why my hands smelled of yeast, and I told him I was only helping until the place closed. I said that for eleven more years.

Who tells a dying man that the salt works he built will be sold by spring? I asked Armand this on my third week, while we raked the evaporation pans outside Beirut and the crust cracked white under our boots. He did not answer. He told me instead to rake slower, so the crystals would not cloud. That evening we carried a tin of the first harvest to Giada's bed, and Armand described the pans to him in detail: how high the brine stood, how the wind had come off the sea. Every word was true. He left out only the letter from the buyers, folded in his breast pocket. Driving back, I said that wasn't lying, exactly. Armand turned the radio up. I have spent years since retelling that drive, and I always slow down at the part where he raked so carefully for a man who would never see the sale.

When Anacleto came up to the terrace on Thursdays, he brought his grammar and, without fail, a small paper of coffee, which he set on the wall beside my inkstand as though it had arrived there by itself. I never thanked him, and he never waited to be thanked. We read our verbs while the bay below us went from grey to silver. Some months before, I had paid the physician who attended his father, and neither of us had spoken of it since; I believed the matter forgotten, as I had wished it to be. This Thursday, however, he recited the conditional mood without a single error and then asked, quite formally, whether I might set him harder lessons, longer ones, as many as I pleased. Rosalinda, my housekeeper, laughed from the doorway at such appetite. I did not laugh. I looked at the coffee on the wall, and then at his careful hands, which had already opened the grammar to a page we had not reached.

On Monday, when I stopped for my mother's mackerel, he wrapped it in a page of newspaper and asked whether the dictionary was heavy. I said it was. He nodded, satisfied, and charged me the usual price, and for years I let my own children believe I had won that contest fair.

Once, when a rumor of a wreck came up the hill, her hands stopped above the threads for a full hour; then she tied the next knot and went on. When you left the noodle stall on Hamra Street last Thursday, Karim, you were certain I had lied to the old cook. I understand why. He asked, in Arabic, whether I was your mother, and you heard me answer with something much longer than 'no.' You assumed I had claimed a title I have not earned. I was annoyed, I admit, that you would not let me explain on the walk home; I even rehearsed a little speech about trust and fairness. But I have since thought about your face at the counter, how quickly the steam hid it, and I am less interested in being right. What I actually said was 'I am the one who gets to feed him today.' My Arabic is clumsy, and perhaps it sounded like more. If it did, I am sorry. Come back to the stall with me on Sunday, and you can ask him yourself what he heard.

Imani

Mumbai has never felt so loud to me as it did this evening on the field behind the school. March 14. I stayed after practice again because Ishaan stays, kicking a ball against the broken goalpost until the light goes orange. Six weeks now without a single word to me, to anyone. I have tried questions, jokes, silence of my own. Tonight I was tired and, honestly, a little resentful; I wrote attendance notes on my knee and told myself a teacher cannot rescue every child. Then the ball rolled to my feet. I pushed it back badly, and he said, 'Your left foot is terrible, Miss Tara.' Five words. I laughed so hard the groundskeeper looked over from the far gate. I am writing this by lamplight and still grinning, though I keep warning myself not to expect another sentence tomorrow.

By the seventh evening of the rains, the people of the lane had made a song about Kwesi. Up the stairs he went to Obinna's projection booth, always with the same cracked lens bundled in a cloth, and down he came with the lens glued and the song a verse longer. Obinna, who mended everything in the old Accra cinema, from ceiling fans to torn reels, played his part well. He sighed loudly, rolled his eyes for the children watching from the steps, and glued. Glass is like a promise, he told them; mend it once and it remembers the break. On the seventh evening, though, he raised the lens into the projector's beam to test his work, and the picture on the screen below came apart into two faces, one bright and one faint. Obinna lowered the lens. The children on the steps stopped singing without being told. In a voice the lane had never heard him use, he asked Kwesi whose film had last passed through this glass, and when Kwesi answered, Obinna wrapped the lens in his own handkerchief.

By noon the barge had run aground on the white crust where the old salt works outside Lyon had flooded and dried a dozen times. Wanjiru, its captain, found the stowaway behind the brine barrels: a girl of perhaps sixteen named Solange, who said she had run from a boarding school and had a little brother waiting at the far landing. Wanjiru meant to march her straight to the gendarmes. Instead, crouched on the salt while the crew dug at the hull, she listened to Solange argue with herself about what to tell the boy. The truth would frighten him; a lie would have to be kept up for years. Wanjiru, who had once told her own sister that their father was merely 'at sea,' found that she had opinions. By the time the barge floated free at dusk, the two of them had written three versions of the story on the back of a cargo manifest, and crossed out every one.

I was nineteen, and Ivan was the name she shouted whenever a clamp slipped, which was often. She was training someone to carry its craft somewhere else after the doors closed.

Grapes do not hurry. So said Vesna, the strictest violin teacher in the hills above Tbilisi, who held her lessons among the vines at harvest so that her pupils would learn patience from the fruit. On the first Tuesday of each month, I fetched my younger brother Wolfram from a reading room near the Ringstrasse in Vienna, where his tutor, Anselm, taught him geography from maps older than our grandparents. Anselm was always late, he hummed while he corrected, and he would not let Wolfram use the tram diagram I had copied out for him. A boy should know a city by its faces, he said, its domes and fountains and shop signs, not by its numbered lines. I told my mother this was an old man's vanity. In February the trams stopped for two days in a snowstorm, and I went out in a panic and found Wolfram already halfway home, steering past the green church dome, the bakery's brass pretzel, the fountain with the chipped nose. I said nothing to Anselm about it the next Tuesday. He was late again, and humming. But I waited for him in the reading room instead of the cold hall, and on the walk home I let Wolfram choose the way.

She was a park ranger then, impatient and sunburned, and she had lent me the money for the bus home without asking my name. Now she was a guest at the next table, laughing too loudly at a toast. I had rehearsed a gracious speech. Instead I pushed through the crowded hall holding a fifty-euro note and stammered something about interest. She looked at the money, then at me, and asked whether I still hiked alone. I admitted that I did. She folded the note back into my hand. 'Then you'll need the bus fare,' she said, and I was too grateful, and too embarrassed, to argue.

Who should stay behind when the olives go down to market? So begin the tellers on the terraces above Naples, and so began young Emilio, newly sent to the hill school, who answered the question with great confidence. The slowest reader, he declared, would stay to mind the trees. Alessia read slowly and counted faster than the priest. She folded her arms and stayed. By noon the baskets at market were tallied wrong, the prices tangled, and Emilio was climbing back up the hill with his collar undone, a climb the tellers describe at length and with evident pleasure. They are careful to add that he asked Alessia's pardon before he asked her help, and that the following year he chose by drawing lots. Some insist he never admitted the error aloud; others say he admitted it only to the trees. Grandmothers telling it still pause here to slice the bread.

and Hollis stood with her hand on its iron door
while Grant, the delivery boy, argued about the boxes:
ten, he said, not twelve; the invoice was wrong.

as if the clay her husband wedged each spring

held the last glaze he had mixed, a blue
she had not dared to open all winter.

Steam rose. One bowl had cracked along the rim.
The others shone. She counted them aloud,
softly, twice, and signed for ten.

count every thread, owe no one, trust no rival.

more than a winter's linen could repay,

Katerina drove the number 12 bus past the harbor in Thessaloniki every morning, and every morning Eda boarded at the stop beside the shoe repair stall. One spring she stepped on carrying a pair of men's brown oxfords, the heels worn to a slant. Her husband had died in January. She had brought the shoes to the cobbler three times, she told Katerina, asking him to replace the soles, then the laces, then the stitching along the toe. Each time he did the work without complaint, and each time she took them home and set them by the door, where no one would wear them. Mending them, Eda said, was like stitching a new sentence onto a closed book. Katerina said nothing and waited at the green light a moment longer than she needed to, so Eda could sit down. Then she pulled away from the curb into the traffic along the sea.

Someone at the fish market had whispered that her late brother once took bribes, a story she had disproved in court decades earlier and never bothered to repeat. Most people shrugged it off. But it reached her niece, who had just been appointed to the bench and who had always believed her uncle was a man without stain. By the next morning, the rumor had found the one door left unlocked, and the niece stopped answering Ingeborg's calls. I, Ingrid, carried the old court file to the niece's office myself, wrapped in brown paper. Ingeborg did not ask whether I had delivered it. She only stood at the railing, watching the gulls ride the wind above the harbor.

Seville's heat had already settled over the terrace when Joaquin carried out the last box. Lucius, his mother's name for the half-built birdhouse they had started when he was nine, still sat on the ledge, its roof missing. She teased him about it while he loaded the car: a future engineer who could not finish four walls and a perch. He laughed, and she laughed louder, listing every project he had abandoned, the kite, the radio, the tiled step. Then she picked up the birdhouse and turned it over in her hands. Underneath, in pencil, were the measurements for the roof, written in his childish script and never used. She stopped talking. She set the birdhouse back on the ledge very carefully, as if it might break, and told him she would leave it exactly as it was until he came home to finish it.

Larissa, who had not set foot in a church in ten years, watched Father Bruno try to arrange one long table for two groups that had never eaten together: the women who kept the old saint's-day customs and the newer members who kept none. He fussed over place cards, shifting names, and Larissa found it absurd, almost comic, that a priest should worry so much about seating. She whispered as much to the woman beside her. Then she noticed what he was doing. He had placed each older weaver beside a newer one whose pattern she had once criticized, and on every plate he had folded a scrap of the other's cloth. Larissa stopped smiling. She saw that the table had been woven as carefully as any shawl on the loom.

I pinned the sheets on Silas's line that spring,
the Cornish wind half wrestling them from me,
and laughed to think how many years we'd spent
at chess-club boards, two old men keeping score
of every bishop lost, each petty win.
He'd beaten me at last the week before.
I meant to tease him over it today.
But in his drawer, beneath the clothespin tin,
I found a notebook of my games, not his,
each losing move of mine marked out in ink
and next to it, in his small careful hand,
the better move, and then: "Show Mabel this."
He never had. The wind went still. I stood
with one white sheet held open in my arms
and folded it as if it were a flag.

Four duties came with my summer job at the rural post office outside Naples: sort the mail, sell the stamps, lock the safe, and give directions to anyone who wandered down from the hills. I was proud of the fourth. So when a hiker named Matteo stumbled in at dusk, sunburned and lost, I drew him a confident map to the trailhead. An hour later Chiara, the park ranger, brought him back. My map had sent him up the wrong ridge. I expected her to tell him whose fault it was. Instead, she told him the trail signs had been moved by the wind, which was not quite true, and she asked me for a glass of water for him. problem.passage:
Before dawn on my tenth birthday, Roxana, the keeper of the bakery in Samarkand, let me in while the ovens were still warming and the air smelled of sesame and smoke. Waya, a surveyor visiting from abroad who lodged upstairs, had brought her a gift: a set of gleaming steel bread stamps, the wrong pattern entirely for our round loaves. Roxana thanked him warmly and pressed one into the first dough of the day, and the bread came out stamped with a foreign star. Waya beamed. I watched her face and saw her mouth tighten, just once, before she laughed and called it lucky. All morning she sold the starred loaves to puzzled customers, explaining with great patience. I remember the courtyard cats waiting by the back door for crumbs.

Which choice best describes the overall mood of the memory?
